analysis.one_liner: Bars banks, credit unions, and credit bureaus from collecting or sharing customers' citizenship or immigration status.
analysis.headline: A Democratic senator introduced the bill in April 2026 with no cosponsors, and it sits in the Senate Banking Committee with no further action as the 119th Congress winds down.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop banks, credit unions, and consumer reporting agencies from asking customers about citizenship or immigration status, keeping or sharing that information, or passing it to federal agencies. It would also bar banking regulators from pressuring institutions to collect such data. Existing anti-money-laundering and sanctions duties would remain in place.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants regardless of legal status, members of mixed-status families, and any consumer who does not want their banking records tied to their citizenship status. The main gain is continued access to basic banking without fear that status information ends up with immigration enforcement.

how_it_helps.text: Covered financial institutions could not require customers to disclose citizenship or immigration status as a condition of opening or keeping an account or accessing a financial service [S2].
They could not collect, record, or retain information about a consumer's citizenship or immigration status at all [S2].
They could not transmit, report, or disclose that information to any federal agency or other governmental entity, cutting off one route by which banking data could reach immigration authorities [S2].
Federal banking regulators would be barred from requiring or encouraging institutions to collect this data or from conditioning approvals and enforcement on such collection or reporting [S2].

The bill explicitly preserves banks' obligations under the Bank Secrecy Act and reporting requirements aimed at money laundering, terrorist financing, and sanctions compliance, so it is a narrower carve-out than a full ban on financial monitoring [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit unions, and consumer reporting agencies would bear the cost of changing data systems and account-opening practices, and could face tension between this ban and existing federal identity-verification rules. Federal agencies would lose a channel of access to immigration-status information held by financial institutions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, credit unions, and credit bureaus

drawbacks.text: Financial institutions already operate under federal rules, including Bank Secrecy Act duties the bill explicitly keeps intact, and banks may still be required to verify identity and legal presence for certain products; the bill could create conflicting mandates and compliance uncertainty for institutions [S2].

Federal immigration and law-enforcement agencies would lose lawful access to information banks currently hold, which supporters of data-sharing argue helps investigations; the bill restricts a government data channel, not just a privacy harm [S2].
With no cosponsors, the bill would face an uphill path in a Senate Banking Committee controlled by the other party, limiting any near-term benefit even in principle [S3] [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it targets, the benefit is concrete: fewer doors closed at the bank teller and less fear that a routine account application becomes an immigration record. The costs are mostly compliance friction for banks, and the bill's carve-outs for anti-money-laundering and sanctions duties mean it does not disable routine financial-crime monitoring. The design is reasonably narrow; the real limitation is political, since it has no cosponsors and no committee movement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and referred to the Banking Committee, which has taken no action on it so far [S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Angela Alsobrooks introduced the bill on April 30, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S4].
The Congress is still in session, so no final outcome has occurred; the bill has not had a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet; the current practice of banks collecting and, where lawful, sharing immigration-status information simply continues while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; status quo continues

for.name: Sen. Angela Alsobrooks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no one besides the sponsor has taken a public position, so no partisan split is visible in the record; the sponsor is a Democrat and the bill has no cosponsors [S3] [S4].

industries.note: They would stop collecting and sharing customers' citizenship data, which cuts both compliance burden and legal exposure on one hand and requires changes to account-opening and data systems on the other. Their interest in reduced regulatory data demands runs alongside customers' privacy here.

Explicitly covered by the bill, they would be barred from holding or disclosing consumers' citizenship or immigration status, removing a data field from their files at some cost to their data-gathering breadth.

industries.industry: Federal immigration and law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill cuts off a channel of access to immigration-status information held by financial institutions, which such agencies could otherwise obtain through legal process or regulator data-sharing.

analysis.trajectory: A first-term bill from a minority-party senator with zero cosponsors and no committee action this late in a Congress rarely advances; the most likely path is that it dies quietly at the end of the session unless the sponsor builds cosponsor support or a related vehicle picks it up.
